overview.text: The Manhattan Project was a top-secret U.S. government program during World War II to develop the first atomic weapons, driven by fear that Nazi Germany might build them first. The Army Corps of Engineers organized it as the Manhattan Engineer District under General Leslie Groves, combining military, scientific, and industrial work across the country. Its three main centers had distinct roles: Oak Ridge enriched uranium, Hanford produced plutonium, and Los Alamos designed the bombs under physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer. On July 16, 1945, the plutonium “Gadget” succeeded in the Trinity test, the first human-caused nuclear explosion. The United States used atomic bombs against Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945; the project helped usher in the nuclear age and raised enduring ethical and environmental questions.

key_facts.text: The project pursued two bomb-making routes in parallel: uranium-235 and plutonium, each requiring different production methods.
The three main sites were not interchangeable: Oak Ridge enriched uranium, Hanford made plutonium, and Los Alamos developed bomb designs.
The federal government acquired the main sites using wartime eminent-domain powers, displacing Indigenous communities, farmers, and homesteaders.
Although the project employed a huge workforce, very few workers knew its true purpose.
After Trinity, the United States dropped the uranium-fueled Little Boy on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, and the plutonium-fueled Fat Man on Nagasaki on August 9.
